edges.description: A viral illness precipitates the acidosis in a child whose mitochondrial oxidative capacity is already limited.

edges.limitations: ThPP is undetectable in null mitochondria but only markedly reduced in patient cells, so the mouse models a more complete depletion than the human disease.
Shown indirectly, through elevated amniotic-fluid 2-oxoglutarate in embryos, rather than by enzyme measurement in situ.
Null embryos die by embryonic day 12 with a neural-tube closure defect, before the period of cortical growth that fails in human patients, so the model cannot show microcephaly or the smooth cortex.

nodes.description: The 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex cannot work without its ThPP cofactor, so 2-oxoglutarate accumulates and is excreted. The enzyme itself is intact: its activity was normal when assayed in patient lymphoblasts, so the defect lies in cofactor supply rather than in the apoenzyme.

evidence.snippet: The reduction of ThPP levels causes dysfunction of the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, which explains the high levels of this organic acid in MCPHA and suggests that mitochondrial ThPP transport is important for CNS development.

nodes.description: Brain growth fails before birth: microcephaly is visible on ultrasound by 21 weeks of gestation and the neonatal brain is smooth and immature, resembling a 20-week fetal brain, with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and, in one patient, partial agenesis of the corpus callosum and a closed spinal dysraphism. The null mouse has a neural-tube closure defect, and knockdown of Slc25a19 in cultured rat neurons reduces dendritic growth. How cofactor deficiency disrupts human brain development has not been shown.

nodes.description: SLC25A19 is the mitochondrial inner-membrane carrier that imports thiamine pyrophosphate, which is synthesised only in the cytosol. The homozygous p.Gly177Ala variant leaves a carrier with negligible transport activity in reconstituted vesicles and reduced abundance in cells. The gene-discovery paper measured deoxynucleotide transport and concluded that the carrier imports deoxynucleotides; the knockout study later showed that nucleotide pools are normal without the carrier and that its substrate is ThPP.

nodes.description: Constitutive Slc25a19 knockout. Homozygous embryos have no detectable mitochondrial ThPP, elevated 2-oxoglutarate in amniotic fluid, a neural-tube closure defect and yolk-sac erythropoietic failure, and all die by embryonic day 12. As a complete null it is more severe than the human hypomorphic genotype and dies before cortical neurogenesis, so it cannot show microcephaly.

GeneReviews recommends oral thiamine (400-600 mg daily, increased during febrile illness or decompensation) for SLC25A19 deficiency as a whole. The reports of benefit come from THMD4, in which high-dose thiamine prevents acute episodes; no report of thiamine treatment in a patient with Amish lethal microcephaly was found (see notes). Whether thiamine can raise mitochondrial ThPP through a carrier with negligible residual activity, or affect a brain malformation that is established before birth, is untested.

nodes.description: Founder missense variant, homozygous in every reported patient. Gly177 is a highly conserved residue in the second signature motif of the mitochondrial carrier family. In reconstituted proteoliposomes the mutant carrier has negligible transport activity; in HepG2 cells it is correctly targeted to mitochondria but is expressed at a reduced level and takes up much less ThPP.
